title: Sorting and the top ten
objectives: Sort results and keep only the first few.
Write clauses in their fixed order, and spot ties at the cut.

screens.prose: Large trades move prices, so a trader checks the busiest days first. The rows below are in the order they were stored, not by size.
screens.question: Tap the volumes of the three busiest rows.

hints.text: Scan the volume column for the largest numbers. All the big ones have six digits.
The VOD rows trade the most shares.
704000, 638000 and 581000 are the three largest. Tap those.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the three largest numbers in the volume column.

byKey.smallest: Those are the three quietest rows. Busiest means the largest volumes.
byKey.r8c3: 527000 is fourth. 704000, 638000 and 581000 are all larger.
byKey.r0c3: 412000 is fifth. Three VOD volumes beat it.

explain.text: You compared every volume to rank them, then kept the top three. Sorting does the comparing, and a cut keeps the top. SQL has a clause for each step.

screens.title: ORDER BY
screens.prose:
`ORDER BY` sorts the result by a column. `DESC` means descending: largest first.

```sql
SELECT date, ticker, volume
FROM prices
ORDER BY volume DESC;
```
screens.question: What is the first row of the result?

options.why: That is the smallest volume, which comes first in ascending order. `DESC` puts the largest first.
That is the first stored row. `ORDER BY` changes the order the rows come back in.

hints.text: Descending means the largest volume leads.
The largest volume in the table is 704000.
704000 belongs to VOD on 2026-03-03.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. `DESC` puts the largest value first.

byKey.stored: That is the first stored row. `ORDER BY` changes the order the rows come back in.

explain.text: `ORDER BY volume DESC` puts the 12 rows in falling order of volume. VOD on 3 March, at 704000, leads. Every row still comes back; only the order changes.

screens.prose:
This time no direction is given:

```sql
SELECT ticker, close
FROM prices
ORDER BY close;
```
screens.question: What is the first tuple in the result?

options.why: You assumed the default is largest first. Without `DESC`, `ORDER BY` sorts ascending, smallest first.
That is the first stored row. `ORDER BY close` reorders the rows by close.

hints.text: What direction does `ORDER BY` use when you do not say?
The default is ascending, written `ASC`: smallest first.
The smallest close is VOD's 0.71 on 3 March.

feedback.correct: Ascending is the default: smallest first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no direction, `ORDER BY` sorts smallest first.

byKey.desc: You assumed the default is largest first. Without `DESC`, `ORDER BY` sorts ascending, smallest first.

explain.text: With no direction, SQL sorts ascending, as if you wrote `ASC`. The smallest close, 0.71, comes first. Python prints the float 26.90 as `26.9`, which is why that option dropped its zero.

screens.title: Two sort keys
screens.prose:
A second column breaks ties in the first. Each column takes its own direction.

```sql
SELECT ticker, date
FROM prices
ORDER BY ticker, date DESC;
```
screens.question: What are the first three rows?

options.why: You applied `DESC` to both columns. It belongs to `date` only, so ticker still sorts A to Z.
You sorted by date first. The first column listed decides; date only breaks ties within a ticker.
That has dates ascending. `DESC` on date puts the newest BARC row first.

hints.text: Sort by the first column. Only when tickers tie does the date matter.
BARC comes first alphabetically. Its three rows tie on ticker.
Within BARC, the dates go newest first: 4, 3, then 2 March.

feedback.correct: Tickers A to Z, and newest first within each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first key decides; `DESC` applies to date alone.

byKey.both-desc: You applied `DESC` to both columns. It belongs to `date` only, so ticker still sorts A to Z.

explain.text: `ticker` sorts A to Z, so the three BARC rows lead. They tie on ticker, so `date DESC` orders them newest first. Each column in `ORDER BY` has its own direction.

screens.title: Keeping the top
screens.prose:
`LIMIT n` keeps the first `n` rows of the sorted result.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
ORDER BY close DESC
LIMIT 4;
```
screens.question: Tap the closes of the four rows it returns.

hints.text: Sort the closes from largest down, then take four.
The three SHEL closes are the largest. The fourth is the best BP close.

feedback.correct: The three SHEL closes and BP's 4.68.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort the closes from largest down, then keep four.

byKey.asc: Those are the four smallest closes. `DESC` sorts largest first.
byKey.first-four: Those are the first four stored rows. `LIMIT` cuts the sorted result, not the table.
byKey.r9c2: 4.66 is BP's second-best close. 4.68 on 2 March is larger and takes fourth place.

explain.text: The sort runs first: 26.90, 26.84, 26.51, 4.68, 4.66 and so on. `LIMIT 4` then keeps the top four rows. BP's 4.66 just misses out.

screens.prose:
A colleague wants the five busiest days and writes:

```sql
SELECT date, ticker, volume
FROM prices
ORDER BY volume
LIMIT 5;
```
screens.question: Does this return the five busiest days?

options.text: No: it returns the five quietest days

options.why: You assumed sorting starts from the top. `ORDER BY` is ascending unless you write `DESC`, so `LIMIT` keeps the smallest volumes.

options.text: No: `LIMIT` runs first, so it sorts the first five stored rows
options.why: SQL sorts the whole result, then `LIMIT` keeps the first rows. The order written is the order applied.

hints.text: Which direction does this `ORDER BY` sort in?
No `DESC`, so ascending: smallest volume first.
The first five rows are the five smallest volumes: 48000 up to 225000.

feedback.correct: Ascending order, so the quietest days come first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the sort direction, then take the first five.

byKey.yes: You assumed sorting starts from the top. `ORDER BY` is ascending unless you write `DESC`, so `LIMIT` keeps the smallest volumes.

explain.text: Without `DESC` the sort is ascending, so the first five rows are the five smallest volumes. `LIMIT` faithfully keeps those. For the busiest days, write `ORDER BY volume DESC LIMIT 5`.

canvas.caption: What it returned: the five quietest rows

screens.title: Ties at the cut
screens.prose:
A dashboard shows one ticker from the latest day:

```sql
SELECT ticker
FROM prices
ORDER BY date DESC
LIMIT 1;
```
screens.question: What does it return?

options.text: One row, and the query does not fix which 4 March ticker it is

options.why: BARC is stored first among the 4 March rows, but four rows tie on date. SQL only promises the order you asked for, so tied rows may come back in any order.

options.text: Four rows: every ticker on the latest date
options.why: `LIMIT 1` keeps one row, even when others tie with it.

hints.text: How many rows share the latest date?
Four rows are dated 2026-03-04. The sort cannot tell them apart.
`LIMIT 1` keeps exactly one, and nothing in the query says which.

feedback.correct: One row, picked from a four-way tie.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many rows tie on the latest date, and what `LIMIT 1` does with them.

byKey.barc: BARC is stored first among the 4 March rows, but four rows tie on date. SQL only promises the order you asked for, so tied rows may come back in any order.

explain.text: Four rows tie on 4 March, and `ORDER BY date DESC` cannot rank them. `LIMIT 1` keeps one, but which is up to the database. Add a second key, such as `ORDER BY date DESC, ticker`, to make the answer fixed.

canvas.caption: Four rows tie on the latest date

screens.prose: You have now used five clauses. SQL fixes the order you write them in, which is also the order the work happens: choose the table, filter, sort, cut.
screens.question: Put the clauses of this query in order: BP's two most recent closes.

hints.text: `SELECT` and `FROM` always open a query.
The filter comes before the sort, and the cut comes last.
`SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Open with `SELECT ... FROM`, then filter, sort and cut.

byKey.limit: `LIMIT` cuts the finished, sorted result, so it goes last.
byKey.where: The filter decides which rows exist to sort, so `WHERE` comes before `ORDER BY`.

explain.text: `WHERE` keeps the three BP rows, `ORDER BY date DESC` puts 4 March first, and `LIMIT 2` keeps two. The result is `('2026-03-04', 4.66)` and `('2026-03-03', 4.61)`.

screens.title: A price series
screens.prose: A backtest computes BP's daily returns, so it needs BP's closes oldest first. Data can arrive late: the tests add a missed BP close for 27 February at the bottom of the table.
screens.question: Make `query()` return the date and close of every BP row, oldest first.

widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests on `db`. They compare the rows your query returns and the column names. Then they add a row to the table and run it again. Rows must match exactly, in order.

hints.text: Filter to BP with `WHERE`, then sort with `ORDER BY`.
Dates are stored as text like `2026-02-27`, which sorts correctly as text. Ascending is the default.
Return the string `SELECT date, close` `FROM prices` `WHERE ticker = 'BP'` `ORDER BY date`.

feedback.correct: Oldest first, even when a row arrives late.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Open the first failing test below the editor.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 wants BP's three rows, date and close, oldest first.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 adds 27 February at the end of the table. Without `ORDER BY date` it comes back last, out of order.

explain.text: `WHERE ticker = 'BP'` keeps three rows and `ORDER BY date` sorts them oldest first. A late row then lands in its proper place. Year-month-day dates sort correctly as text, which is why databases store them that way.

screens.title: Busiest days
screens.prose: A market-impact check looks at the five busiest rows before sizing a trade. The tests also add a VOD day with 912000 shares, which should go straight to the top.
screens.question: Make `query()` return the date, ticker and volume of the five rows with the largest volume, largest first.

widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests on `db`. They compare the rows your query returns and the column names. Then they add a row to the table and run it again. Rows must match exactly, in order.

hints.text: Sort by volume, in the right direction, then cut.
Busiest first needs `DESC`. Five rows needs `LIMIT 5`.
Return the string `SELECT date, ticker, volume` `FROM prices` `ORDER BY volume DESC` `LIMIT 5`.

feedback.correct: The five busiest rows, largest first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Open the first failing test below the editor.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects 704000 first and 412000 fifth. Smallest volumes first means `DESC` is missing.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 adds a 912000 day. It must come first and push 412000 out.

explain.text: `ORDER BY volume DESC` ranks every row by volume, largest first. `LIMIT 5` keeps the top five, from 704000 down to 412000. The new 912000 day takes first place and BARC's 412000 drops out.

ideas: `ORDER BY` sorts the result, ascending unless you write `DESC`. Each sort column takes its own direction.
`LIMIT n` keeps the first `n` rows of the sorted result; it ranks nothing by itself.
Clauses go `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`: filter, then sort, then cut.

formula.name: Top n
formula.note: Add a second sort key when ties could straddle the cut.

summary.trap: `ORDER BY volume LIMIT 5` gives the five quietest days. The busiest need `DESC`.

quiz.prose: A table `prices` holds 250 rows for one ticker, one per trading day. You want the ten most recent rows.
quiz.question: Which query returns them?

options.why: That sorts oldest first, so `LIMIT` keeps the first ten days of the history.
Without `ORDER BY`, SQL promises no order. You usually get the first ten stored rows.
`LIMIT` must come last. This one is a syntax error.

feedback.correct: Newest first, then cut at ten.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort newest first, then keep ten.

explain.text: `ORDER BY date DESC` puts the newest day first and `LIMIT 10` keeps ten. They come back newest first; reverse them in Python if you need date order.

quiz.prose:
`prices` has 12 rows.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
ORDER BY close
LIMIT 20;
```
quiz.question: How many rows come back?

feedback.correct: `LIMIT` is a ceiling, not a target.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `LIMIT 20` keeps at most 20 rows.

byKey.twenty: There are only 12 rows. `LIMIT` cannot invent more.
byKey.none: Asking for more rows than exist is not an error. You get all 12.

explain.text: `LIMIT 20` keeps up to 20 rows. The table has only 12, so all 12 come back, sorted by close.

options.text: Three rows, in whatever order the database reads them, usually the first three stored
The three rows with the largest closes
options.why: You assumed `LIMIT` picks the best rows. It only cuts; without `ORDER BY` nothing is ranked.
Nothing here mentions the date. Without `ORDER BY`, recent rows have no priority.

feedback.correct: A cut with no sort is just the first rows read.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `LIMIT` cuts, it does not rank.

explain.text: `LIMIT` keeps the first rows of whatever order the result has. With no `ORDER BY`, that is the order the database reads them, usually storage order. Always sort before you take a top `n`.

quiz.prose:
`prices` holds BARC, BP, SHEL and VOD. VOD closed at 0.72, 0.71 and 0.73.

```sql
SELECT ticker, close
FROM prices
ORDER BY ticker DESC, close;
```
quiz.question: What is the first tuple?

options.why: `DESC` belongs to `ticker` only. Within VOD, close sorts ascending, so 0.71 leads.
`DESC` on ticker puts Z before A, so VOD comes first, not BARC.

feedback.correct: VOD first, then its smallest close.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort tickers Z to A, then closes smallest first.

explain.text: `ticker DESC` sorts Z to A, so VOD leads. Within VOD, `close` has no direction, so it sorts ascending and 0.71 comes first.
